THIS CRIMINAL REVISION PETITION HAVING BEEN HEARD AND  RESERVED ON 15-12-2023, COMING ON FOR PRONOUNCEMENT, THIS  DAY, THE COURT PRONOUNCED THE FOLLOWING:
 -2-  NC: 2024:KHC:14379  CRL.RP No. 1295 of 2019  ORDER Heard Sri P. B. Umesh, learned counsel for the petitioner/accused and Sri Vinay Mahadevaiah,
learned High Court Government Pleader for the respondent-State.
2.

The petitioner/accused has preferred this revision petition under Section 397 read with Section 401 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, (for short, 'Cr.P.C') praying to set aside the judgment of conviction and order on sentence dated 27-7-2017 passed by the Principal Civil Judge and Judicial Magistrate of First Class, Chitradurga (for short, 'trial Court'), in Criminal Case No.669 of 2007, which is confirmed by the II Additional District and Sessions Judge, Chitradurga (for short,
'First Appellate Court'), in Criminal Appeal No.46 of 2017 dated 26-9-2019, wherein both the Courts passed concurrent findings in respect of the offences punishable under Sections 420, 468, 471 and 473 of the Indian Penal Code,1860 (for short, 'IPC') and convicted the accused for the aforesaid offences.

sentences.text: For the sake of convenience, the parties are referred to as per their rankings before the trial Court.
The petitioner is the sole accused and the respondent is the complainant-State before the trial Court.

4. The brief facts of the prosecution case are as under:
On 29-11-2014, the accused opened a savings bank account at Syndicate Bank,
Chitradurga.

At the time of opening his account, he submitted his service certificate by forging the same as being issued by Smt. Shantha, Head Mistress, Government Higher Primary School, Siddapur, Chitradurga, with forged signature.

Further, soon after opening the account, the accused mentioned account No.40601 belonged to some other person on cheque leaf No.161858 and used the said cheque leaf as genuine and presented it for encashment of Rs.65,000/-
on 17-10-2005 by forging the signature of one Thipperudrappa, thereby, the accused cheated the Bank NC: 2024:KHC:14379 Authorities and one of its customers.

Hence,
the Bank Manager lodged a complaint on 23.11.2005 as per Ex.P3 and this led to registration of F.I.R. and investigation.

The Investigating Officer filed the charge-sheet against the accused for the offences punishable under Sections 465,
468, 471, 473 and 420 of IPC and the learned Magistrate framed charges against the M T Ravikumar vs The State Of Karnataka on 14 March, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/85476006/
2 accused for the aforesaid offences.

sentences.text: 5. The prosecution, in order to bring home the guilt of the accused, examined in all eight witnesses as PWs.1 to 8 and got marked fifty-one documents as per Exs.P1 to P51.
The case of the accused was one of total denial.
For the defence, the accused did not enter the witness box and did not produce any documents.
The trial Court based on the oral and documentary evidence on record, convicted the accused for the offences punishable under Sections 468, 471, 473 and 420 of IPC.

Further the trial Court sentenced the accused to various terms of sentence and imprisonment as below:
NC: 2024:KHC:14379
Convicted for the Sl. offence Order on Fine in Default No.

punishable Sentence Rs. Sentence under Section 1. 420 of IPC Simple 5,000/- Simple imprisonment imprisonment for 1 year for 3 months 2. 468, 471 Rigorous 5,000/- Simple and 473 of imprisonment for each imprisonment IPC for 2 years of the for 3 months for each of offences the offence All the sentences were ordered to run concurrently.

6. Aggrieved by the judgment of conviction and order on sentence passed by the trial Court, the accused preferred Criminal Appeal No.46 of 2017 before the First Appellate Court and the First Appellate Court dismissed the appeal and confirmed the judgment of conviction and order on sentence passed by the trial Court.

7. Learned counsel for the petitioner/accused contended that the impugned order of conviction and sentence passed by the trial Court which is confirmed by the First Appellate Court is contrary to law,
evidence on record and probabilities of the case; the Courts below have NC: 2024:KHC:14379 committed serious error in convicting the accused on the prosecution evidence which is highly interested, contradictory and unreliable.
It is contended that the prosecution is guilty of suppression of material evidence and has not come forward with the true version of the incident.
The Courts below have committed serious error in holding that the prosecution has proved beyond reasonable doubt that the accused is guilty of the offences alleged against him.
8. Further, there is a long delay in filing the complaint and the delay has been conveniently used by the prosecution to suit its case.

The Courts below have committed serious error by relying on the evidence of PWs.1 to 4, who are interested witnesses and hence, their testimonies are not consistent and cogent and they are full of material contradictions and omissions.

It is further contended that the Courts below ought to have acquitted the accused on the ground that Exs.P1 and Ex.P6 were not produced by the accused and the evidence of PW8 is in the NC: 2024:KHC:14379 nature of opinion and same is hit by Sections 45 and 73 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 (for short, 'Evidence Act').

In so far as Exs.P1 and P6 are concerned, it can be inferred that the prosecution had relied upon inadmissible documents in support of its case and failed to prove its case by adducing cogent and reliable evidence, which goes to the very root of the case.

sentences.text: It is contended that the Courts below ought to have acquitted the accused on the ground that the prosecution has failed to take note of the absence of the material evidence, such as, opening of savings bank account papers, examination of introducer to open the account, the Officer who opened savings bank account to substantiate that the disputed Service Certificate-Ex.P6 which was produced to the Bank by the accused and also to prove that the accused had an account in the complainant's Bank.

As such, the conclusion of the trial Court that Ex.P6-Service Certificate belongs to the accused is erroneous and the prosecution has wrongly relied on NC: 2024:KHC:14379 evidence of PW8 and come to the wrong conclusion to hold the accused is found guilty.

10. It is contended that the Courts below have erred in convicting the accused relying on the evidence of PW8 and FSL report and his opinion report at Exs.P50 and P51 in the absence of any material to show that specimen writings and signatures are of the accused and documents at Exs.P44 to P49 and P24 to P32 are hit by Sections 45 and 73 of the Evidence Act.
It is further contended that, PWs.6 and 7, whose signature and account in the Bank are alleged to be used/forged by the accused, have not supported the case of the prosecution.

11. It is contended that the Courts below ought to have appreciated the defence taken by the accused that Ex.P6-Service Certificate did not bear any signature of any official of the Bank and seal of the Bank and it did not contain any identity of the person related to it, such as name of the father, age,
etc. so that the prosecution fails to prove to connect Ex.P6-Service Certificate to the NC:
2024:KHC:14379 accused and the Courts below without considering these aspects erroneously held that the accused is guilty of the alleged offences.

It is contended that the Courts below have erred in convicting the accused in the absence of any offences committed by the accused much less the offence alleged against him and thus, ingredients of offences punishable under Sections 468, 471,
473 and 420 of IPC have not proved by the prosecution.
12.

It is contended that the trial Court has committed great error in convicting the accused since the Investigating Officer was not examined during the trial and the charge-sheet witnesses namely viz.,
CWs.2, 5, 10 and 13 including the independent witnesses have not been examined during the trial.

13. It is contended that the Courts below have committed serious error in convicting the accused on the document at Ex.P2, wherein the author of the said document has not supported the prosecution case fully.
Under the facts and circumstances, it can be inferred that prosecution has not come forward with true version of the incident.
It is contended that if the evidence of the prosecution is taken on its face value, nowhere the ingredients of Sections 468, 471, 473 and 420 of IPC are proved with respect to the accused.
Hence, the accused has to be acquitted as he has not committed any offences or even was remotely to commit.

14. Learned High Court Government Pleader has contended that the judgment and order of conviction and sentence passed by both the Courts is in accordance with law; both the Courts have M T Ravikumar vs The State Of Karnataka on 14 March, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/85476006/
4 assigned proper and acceptable reasons while imposing sentence on the accused; both the Courts have taken into consideration the gravity of offences committed against the Bank and its customer by producing forged document.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
Hence, the accused has committed the offences which are serious in nature and he has cheated the Bank and its customer by producing forged Ex.P6-Service Certificate;
both the Courts have - 11 - NC: 2024:KHC:14379 considered this aspect of the matter and have rightly convicted the accused.
On all these grounds, he prays to reject the petition.

15. On the basis of the above, the following point arises for the consideration of this Court:
i. Whether the judgment of conviction and order on sentence passed by the trial Court and confirmed by the First Appellate Court calls for interference?
16.

The Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of MUNNA DEVI v. STATE OF RAJASTHAN AND ANOTHER reported in (2001) 9 SCC 631 while discussing the scope of Section 397 of Cr.P.C. held at paragraph No.3 as under:
"3. xxx xxx xxx.

entities.text: MUNNA DEVI v. STATE OF RAJASTHAN AND ANOTHER reported in (2001) 9 SCC 631
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The revision power under the Code of Criminal Procedure cannot be exercised in a routine and casual manner.
While exercising such powers the High Court has no authority to appreciate the evidence in the manner as the trial and the appellate courts are required to do.

Revisional powers - 12 - NC: 2024:KHC:14379 could be exercised only when it is shown that there is a legal bar against the continuance of the criminal proceedings or the framing of charge or the facts as stated in the first information report even if they are taken at the face value and accepted in their entirety do not constitute the offence for which the accused has been charged."
17.

The Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of STATE OF TAMIL NADU v. R. SOUNDIRARASU AND OTHERS reported in (2023) 6 SCC 768 at paragraph No.79 held as under:
"79.

entities.text: STATE OF TAMIL NADU v. R. SOUNDIRARASU AND OTHERS reported in (2023) 6 SCC 768
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Thus, the revisional power cannot be exercised in a casual or mechanical manner.
It can only be exercised to correct manifest error of law or procedure which would occasion injustice, if it is not corrected.
The revisional power cannot be equated with appellate power.
A Revisional Court cannot undertake meticulous examination of the material on record as it is undertaken by the trial court or the appellate court.

This power can only be exercised if there is any legal bar to the continuance of the M T Ravikumar vs The State Of Karnataka on 14 March, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/85476006/
5 - 13 - NC: 2024:KHC:14379 proceedings or if the facts as stated in the charge-sheet are taken to be true on their face value and accepted in their entirety do not constitute the offence for which the accused has been charged.

entities.text: M T Ravikumar vs The State Of Karnataka
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: It is conferred to check grave error of law or procedure."

18. Further, the Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of STATE OF MAHARASHTRA v. SUJAY MANGESH POYAREKAR reported in (2008) 9 SCC 475 at paragraph No.16 held as under:
"16. xxx xxx xxx.

entities.text: STATE OF MAHARASHTRA v. SUJAY MANGESH POYAREKAR reported in (2008) 9 SCC 475
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Now it is well settled that revisional jurisdiction can be exercised sparingly and only in exceptional cases.
A Revisional Court cannot convert itself into a regular court of appeal."

19. Therefore, the revisional jurisdiction should normally be exercised in exceptional cases, when there is a glaring defect in the proceedings or there is a manifest error of point of law and consequently, there has been a flagrant miscarriage of justice.
In view of the above proposition of law, let me examine the case of the prosecution.

21. It is the case of the prosecution that on 29-11-2014, the accused while opening his savings bank account at Syndicate Bank, Chitradurga, had produced Ex.P6 forged Service Certificate purporting it to be issued by the Head Mistress of Higher Primary School, Siddapur, Chitradurga.

Further, the accused obtained Ex.P1-cheque leaf bearing No.161858 and used it as genuine document and presented for encashment of Rs.65,000/- on 17-10-2005 by forging the signature of one Thipperudrappa, thereby the accused cheated the Bank and one of its customers.

On perusal of the evidence of PW1- Satyabodacharya, then Branch Manager of Syndicate Bank at relevant point of time, has stated that Ex.P1-cheque leaf was issued in favour of the accused,
wherein Account No.40601 shown was issued in the name of the accused, but he has not stated as to Ex.P6-Service Certificate - 15 - NC: 2024:KHC:14379 produced at the time of opening the bank account.
Hence, he turned hostile to the case of the prosecution.
In the cross-examination, he admits that he came to know that the accused forged the signature of one Thipperudrappa on Ex.P1-cheque leaf and presented it for encashment to the Bank.

His further evidence is that he made enquiry as to the documents furnished at the time of opening of bank M T Ravikumar vs The State Of Karnataka on 14 March, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/85476006/
6 account and he noticed that at the time of opening bank account also, the accused furnished forged Ex.P6-Service Certificate.
b. PW2-M. Kemparaju, Assistant Senior Bank Manager-cum-complainant has stated that he came to know about the act of the accused.

sentences.text: Hence, he lodged the complaint to the Police as per Ex.P3.

The Police visited the Bank, seized Ex.P1-cheque leaf and Ex.P6-Service Certificate while drawing spot and seizure panchanama- Ex.P4.
- 16 - NC: 2024:KHC:14379 c. PW3-P. Thimmappa has stated that the Police have conducted seizure mahazar as per Ex.P4 in his presence and seized Ex.P1-cheque and Ex.P6-Service Certificate dated 22-11-2004.
He has further stated that the accused had furnished Ex.P6 at the time of opening of Bank account.
d. PW4-Somashekaraiah, a witness to Ex.P2-spot cum seizure mahazar has stated that the Police conducted seizure mahazar in his presence and seized Ex.P1-cheque and Ex.P6-Service Certificate.

e. PW5-M. Shyalaja, Head Mistress of Higher Primary School, Siddapura, Chitradurga, has stated that as per the records maintained in her School, a Teacher by name Ravi Kumar, and a Head Mistress, by name Shanthamma, never worked in the Higher Primary School, Siddapura,
Chitradurga.

f. PW6-Somashekharappa, a customer of Syndicate Bank, in whose account a sum of Rs.65,000/-
was drawn,
- 17 - NC: 2024:KHC:14379 has turned hostile.
He denied in the cross-examination that in Ex.P1-cheque leaf, his signature was affixed as Thipperudrappa which belonged to the accused.
g. PW7-Zakeer Hussain is a witness to seizure mahazar.
He has stated that the Police never conducted seizure panchanama in his presence as per Ex.P4 in the house of the accused.
Thereby, he has turned hostile to the case of the prosecution.
h. PW8-Syed Azgar Imam, Scientific Officer and Handwriting Expert, FSL, Bengaluru, has stated that he examined Ex.P6 which was fabricated and signature was forged.

Hence, he issued his report as per Ex.P50.
23.

Learned counsel for the petitioner has contended that the prosecution witnesses, during the course of their cross-examination, have pleaded their ignorance as to the date, number and other particulars.
This case is based on documentary evidence.

More particularly, all material - 18 - M T Ravikumar vs The State Of Karnataka on 14 March, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/85476006/
7 NC: 2024:KHC:14379 witnesses were examined after lapse of a decade and therefore, one cannot expect from them to give accurate details as to dates, numbers and other particulars in respect of disputed cheque.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: He further contended with vehemence that, no conviction can be imposed on the accused on the basis of expert opinion.
24. In fact, the expert opinion must always be received with great caution and it is unsafe to base a conviction solely on expert opinion without substantial corroboration.
This ratio is laid down in case of S. GOPAL REDDY v. STATE OF A.P. reported in (1996) 4 SCC 596.

entities.text: S. GOPAL REDDY v. STATE OF A.P. reported in (1996) 4 SCC 596
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
Whereas in the instant case, the prosecution is not relying upon the evidence of expert opinion,
PW8.

In fact, the evidence of expert witness is corroborated with the evidence of other witnesses,
who have clearly spoken regarding the alleged act of the accused.
There is much corroboration from the other material available on record.
Learned counsel for the petitioner contended that the prosecution has not furnished details about a boy through whom Ex.P1-cheque was presented.
As per the prosecution case, the boy, who had presented the cheque, ran away from the Bank.
The prosecution neither secured the presence of said boy nor provided any details about him.
Admittedly, there are some lapses on the part of the Investigating Officer.
Merely because the Investigating Officer committed error, the same cannot be doubted and the same is not fatal to the case of the prosecution.
Mere fault or improper investigation will not absolve the accused of his guilt.

The prosecution witnesses have established the fact that the cheque was presented through a boy, but the fact remains that, it was the accused who was the beneficiary and hence, the accused had forged the signature on Ex.P1-cheque and also fabricated Ex.P6- Service Certificate.
Hence, there is no merit consideration in the contention of the learned counsel for the petitioner.
He further contended that the cheque was not misused and Service Certificate was not forged.

But, the material - 20 - NC: 2024:KHC:14379 available on record clearly establishes that the Service Certificate submitted by him to the Bank authorities and cheque leaf issued to him was also misused.
Under such circumstances, the accused has to explain as to how and who has misused Ex.P1-cheque and Ex.P6-Service Certificate.
But, the accused has not furnished any explanation in this regard.
The stand of accused is of total denial.
In view of Section 106 of Evidence Act, when any fact is especially within the knowledge of any person, the burden of proving that fact is upon him.
No explanation of whatsoever is forthcoming from the accused in this regard except bare denial.
Thus for all these reasons, there is no other view to be inferred from the material on record that the accused is guilty of committing the alleged act.

sentences.text: On perusal of the evidence of PWs.1 to 5, they have deposed about the production of Exs.P1-cheque leaf and P6-Service Certificate produced by the accused and the purpose of forgery and the manner of using those documents, at the relevant point of time.
Their oral - 21 - NC: 2024:KHC:14379 testimonies are clear and corroborative in nature.
They have clearly stated that the accused forged the document in order to open the Bank account and to withdraw the amount from other customer's account of Syndicate Bank.

On perusal of the judgment passed by the trial Court as well as the First Appellate Court, it appears that the accused has furnished forged Service Certificate-Ex.P6 and opened the Bank account and later, Ex.P1-cheque leaf which was issued by the Bank in his favour, misused it by writing the name of one Thipperudrappa as if it belonged to him and mentioned Account No.40601 of Somashekarappa-PW6.
Hence, it clearly transpires that the accused has committed the offences and cheated the Bank by producing forged documents in order to cheat the customer of Syndicate Bank.
Therefore, the trial Court as well as the First Appellate Court have rightly convicted the accused for the aforesaid offences.
Learned counsel for the petitioner contended that the Investigating Officer has not followed the procedure, no mahazar is drawn while taking specimen signature.
28. If investigation is illegal or suspicious, the rest of the evidence must be scrutinised independently.

In this case, the trial Court and the First Appellate Court convinced that the accused had furnished forged document in order to open his savings Bank account and subsequently, forged the signature of customer of the Bank in the cheque-leaf issued by the Bank in favour of the accused.
As per the evidence of PW8-Scientific Officer and Hand Writing expert, Ex.P6 was forged document and it can be seen in FSL report-Ex.P50.
Hence, there is no merit in his contention.
29 . It is contended that the trial Court framed charge for Section 468 of IPC and it was defective one.
From perusal of the charge, the trial Court framed charge for Section 468 of IPC as the accused committed forgery of - 23 - NC: 2024:KHC:14379 Ex.P1-cheque as well as the Service Certificate-Ex.P6.

Hence, the trial Court properly framed the charge for the offence punishable under Section 468 of IPC.
30.
It is contended that there is delay in lodging the complaint.

As per the case of the prosecution,
the accused opened the savings bank account on 29-11-2004, the cheque-leaf presented on 17-10-2005 before the Syndicate Bank for encashment of Rs.65,000/- and withdrew the same.
The complaint was lodged on 23-11-2005.

Admittedly, the accused cheated the Bank by forging the M T Ravikumar vs The State Of Karnataka on 14 March, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/85476006/
9 signature of one of the customers and caused loss for a tune of Rs.65,000/-.

entities.text: M T Ravikumar vs The State Of Karnataka
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: This fact came to the knowledge of the Bank Authorities in the month of November, 2005 and hence, there was delay on the part of the Bank Authorities to ascertain the person who caused loss to the Bank and in this process, there is delay in lodging the complaint and the delay is properly explained.
31. It is contended that Ex.P1-cheque leaf belonged to one Thipperudrappa and he is cited as CW5.

However,
- 24 - NC: 2024:KHC:14379 the prosecution has not examined him and Ex.P1 was produced by a boy, but the said boy has not been examined.
If CW5 is an aggrieved party and he is not examined, the accused cannot be acquitted on the sole ground of non-examination of the victim.
In fact, the accused caused inconvenience and lower the reputation of the Bank by furnishing forged documents and used it as genuine document for his benefit.
Hence, non-examination of loser of the amount from the Bank cannot vitiate the trial.
Further, merely because a minor boy produced Ex.P1-cheque leaf for encashment, the accused cannot be escaped from liability and non-examination of the boy is not fatal to the case of the prosecution.
32. It is contended that one Shantha, Head Mistress of Higher Primary School, not examined and on the other hand, one Shylaja of the said School has been examined.

From perusal of the evidence of PW5, it reveals that as per the records maintained in the School, a Teacher by name Ravi Kumar,
and a Head Mistress, by name Shanthamma,
- 25 - NC: 2024:KHC:14379 never worked in the Higher Primary School, Siddapur, Chitradurga Taluk.
Therefore, the question of examining said Shantha is not at all necessary.
If the Investigating Officer is not questioned on this aspect, disbelieving a prosecution witness, on that score, is improper.
33. Learned counsel for the petitioner has contended in vehemence that the trial Court has not heard on sentence as contemplated under Section 248(2) of Cr.P.C.
Hence, the entire proceedings liable to be vitiated.
34. Perused the order-sheet maintained by the trial Court in Criminal Case No.669 of 2007.

On 27-7-2017, the trial Court heard the matter on sentence in detail from the learned counsel for the accused and the learned Additional Public Prosecutor for the State, but the trial Court failed to incorporate the portion of hearing on sentence in the operative portion of its judgment dated 27-7-2017.

Therefore, the accused cannot take an undue advantage that the trial Court did not afford an opportunity to him - 26 - M T Ravikumar vs The State Of Karnataka on 14 March, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/85476006/
10 NC: 2024:KHC:14379 while hearing on sentence.

entities.text: M T Ravikumar vs The State Of Karnataka
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Hence, there is no merit in the contention of the learned counsel for the petitioner in this regard.
35. Looking into any angle, there are no grounds to hold that the judgment of conviction and order on sentence passed by the trial Court is improper.
The Court is satisfied that there is no glaring defect in the proceedings and there is no manifest error of point of law.

36. In view of the facts and circumstances of the case and the concurrent findings passed by the trial Court and the First Appellate Court, the Court is of the view that the revision petition is liable to be dismissed.

37. In the result, the Court proceeds to pass the following:
ORDER Criminal Revision Petition filed by the petitioner/accused is dismissed.

opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
19. Therefore, the revisional jurisdiction should normally be exercised in exceptional cases, when there is a glaring defect in the proceedings or there is a manifest error of point of law and consequently, there has been a flagrant miscarriage of justice.
This ratio is laid down in case of S. GOPAL REDDY v. STATE OF A.P. reported in (1996) 4 SCC 596.
In fact, the evidence of expert witness is corroborated with the evidence of other witnesses,
who have clearly spoken regarding the alleged act of the accused.
The prosecution neither secured the presence of said boy nor provided any details about him.
Merely because the Investigating Officer committed error, the same cannot be doubted and the same is not fatal to the case of the prosecution.
Mere fault or improper investigation will not absolve the accused of his guilt.
The prosecution witnesses have established the fact that the cheque was presented through a boy, but the fact remains that, it was the accused who was the beneficiary and hence, the accused had forged the signature on Ex.P1-cheque and also fabricated Ex.P6- Service Certificate.
But, the accused has not furnished any explanation in this regard.
The stand of accused is of total denial.
In view of Section 106 of Evidence Act, when any fact is especially within the knowledge of any person, the burden of proving that fact is upon him.
No explanation of whatsoever is forthcoming from the accused in this regard except bare denial.
Hence, it clearly transpires that the accused has committed the offences and cheated the Bank by producing forged documents in order to cheat the customer of Syndicate Bank.
Therefore, the trial Court as well as the First Appellate Court have rightly convicted the accused for the aforesaid offences.
In this case, the trial Court and the First Appellate Court convinced that the accused had furnished forged document in order to open his savings Bank account and subsequently, forged the signature of customer of the Bank in the cheque-leaf issued by the Bank in favour of the accused.
Hence, the trial Court properly framed the charge for the offence punishable under Section 468 of IPC.
30.
Hence, non-examination of loser of the amount from the Bank cannot vitiate the trial.
Further, merely because a minor boy produced Ex.P1-cheque leaf for encashment, the accused cannot be escaped from liability and non-examination of the boy is not fatal to the case of the prosecution.
Hence, the entire proceedings liable to be vitiated.
On 27-7-2017, the trial Court heard the matter on sentence in detail from the learned counsel for the accused and the learned Additional Public Prosecutor for the State, but the trial Court failed to incorporate the portion of hearing on sentence in the operative portion of its judgment dated 27-7-2017.
Therefore, the accused cannot take an undue advantage that the trial Court did not afford an opportunity to him - 26 - M T Ravikumar vs The State Of Karnataka on 14 March, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/85476006/
